Totals of 2021
8 February 2022 ·

It is a bit late to sum up, isn't it? Well, the previous couple of months have been, um, tight, so I had no actual time to sit down and think. Now I'm on vacation for 2021 – so no time like the present. I'm writing, like, from the past.

Write out each achievement doesn't attract me at all. The year definitely turned out to be good: I did a lot of complex work on FirstBit ERP (wrote new modules, rewrote existing ones, crushed bugs, wrote functional and load tests – yes, there were countless things). This had a good effect both on the configuration itself and on the profits of my company. In addition, I passed 1C expert exam and a PostgreSQL professional exam. Hip-hip-hooray.

There were fails as well. I still feel lazy to jot them down, but the main one is obvious – I became monstrously fat and instead of losing ten kilograms (that was the original plan) – I gained five more.

Looking back, the root of most of the problems over the past year is this: I focused too much on task flow. They were all interesting in their own way, from a carefully written technical task to challenges like “find a problem in the code using your witcher's instincts”. You do one task, another, a third, a hundredth, and you do not notice that you have ignored almost everything except work. As a result, you get a lot of experience, but the world dries up to the Configurator window and there is no strength to somehow apply this experience. Unhealthy bullshit.

In short, if you imagine me as a character in some video game, it looks like this: attack and intelligence have grown noticeably over the year, but health, agility, charisma, and almost everything else in general, have dropped. Now I need to do something to deal with this mess.

You know what? I'll take ten kilometers run for a start.

Maybe, birdie, maybe.

Reuse Carefully
8 February 2022 ·

I'll tell you about a funny and a little embarrassing case that I took apart in January. The essence in a nutshell: a huge auto-test based on Vanessa, which is intended to check the VAT calculation, falls somewhere near the end.

I start investigating. First, I look at the screenshots in Allure: OK, the reason is obvious – in one of the documents, the conditional appearance for the field with the VAT amount doesn't work. The test expected it to be unavailable if the VAT rate is zero, but it turned out to be available somehow.

It's a mess, it needs to be fixed! I look at the condition in the code: well, it locks the field if the VAT rate is in the list of “zero” rates (list of VAT rates whose rate is equal to zero). Everything appears to be simple and logical. What the hell could possibly go wrong here?

Well, I try to reproduce the bug manually. And there, all of a sudden, everything is nice: the conditional appearance works as it should. Floating bug, or what? I run the auto-test again, at the right moment I jump in with the debugger and find some outright garbage: in the list of “zero” rates, besides themselves, there are a bunch of empty links!

Frankly speaking, I was scratching the back of my head. The document receives this list from the common module with this code. An empty ref from here, even theoretically, cannot be obtained. Moreover, the module has the “Reuse Return Values” option ​​enabled, and the function is actually executes once somewhere at the beginning of the test, before all complex data manipulations. So, the test cannot affect it in any way, in theory.

Is it a dead end? Well, experienced colleagues have probably already guessed everything, but I had to dance around the bug and even check the standard, until got the following: return values ​​cache in 1C can be changed. I mean, not by calling RefreshReusableValues​​(), but by changing reusable values directly.

How? Well, if you get some values ​​from a cached common module, and they are not of a primitive type (string, number, etc.), you will not get the value itself, but a pointer to it somewhere in memory. You write this pointer to a variable and try to change it – you change the cache.

It's that simple, yes. This is what happened in my case: the form of another document called the method that generates the list of “zero” rates. Having received a list of values, it added an empty ref to it and used it in its logic. Thus, each time this form opens, the list cache contains more and more empty refs, which eventually broke the document at the other end of the configuration.

In a good way, the platform should throw exceptions when developer trying to change the cache, but until this happens, you have to take care yourself. For example, when developing cached modules, return immutable data types from them (FixedStructure instead of Structure, FixedArray instead of Array, and so on). True, this is not a 100% protection: firstly, fixed types are not applicable everywhere, and secondly, even in the latest versions of the SSL, this is far from being done everywhere. Do you know many configurations not based on SSL?

Sonar also know nothing about the problem, as well as less popular software. No silver bullet, in short – check your code, look at the code of your colleagues and try not to forget about another elegant way to bang ourselves in the foot.

Second Monitor Management via Console
16 October 2021 ·

I have two monitors. I use the second one during meetings in Zoom or when playing together with friends (in both cases it's convenient to bring the people's cameras there). There are more examples when it's useful, but often the device is simply idle. In order not to be distracted, I decided to turn it off.

What is the ambush here: it is inconvenient to enable or disable the second monitor via OS (a few clicks, and you need to scroll, and all the time you get confused where to go — in “Screen settings” or “Personalization”). I would like one command, and the command on a hotkey. And, ideally, from the script to rule all this.

I did not find the script, but I found a ready-made utility — MultiMonitorTool. It's free. Works under the Windows 10 without problems. The commands below turn on / off the 2nd monitor:

MultiMonitorTool.exe / disable 2
MultiMonitorTool.exe / enable 2
MultiMonitorTool.exe / switch 2

For some reason, when you turn on a monitor via enable or switch, it's positioned incorrectly sometimes (for example, before it was turned off, it was on the right, and after turning it on, it was on the left). This is fixable. First, let's save the configuration at the moment when both monitors are on:

MultiMonitorTool.exe / SaveConfig Monitors.cfg

And then, when you need to turn on the monitor, load the saved config:

MultiMonitorTool.exe / LoadConfig Monitors.cfg

The utility can do a lot more (for example, one of the commands flips application windows between monitors). Follow the link above for the description.

Building The Blog on GitHub
29 September 2021 ·

For the last year this site has been working on a simple platform: statics, GitHub and my domain. All the pages were pre-generated and placed in a GitHub's repository with GitHub Pages enabled.

I collected statics using a script. It was working with a list of text files, pedantically arranged in folders. The script rummaged through them and generated HTML files. Then I manually pushed them to the repository.

This scheme worked well, but the number of clicks annoyed me. Here is the script pull, and there is the script pull, and then you have to tinker with the git. I wanted it to be simpler.

At some point, I figured out that not only the deployment of statics, but also the assembly can be shifted onto the shoulders of GitHub. I put together some thoughts and added two more repositories:

  1. A repository of initial data. Here I put the content of the site: the text files and a bit of metadata (page titles, dates of pages creation, tags for notes, and so on).
  2. A repository of the script for generating statics. In addition to the script itself, I put various assets here (icons, styles, manifests — in general, everything that doesn't need to be generated every time, but you have to “put” it next to the resulting HTML).

Then I wrote an action that wakes up with every push to the repository with the initial data. Shortly, its logic:

  1. Clone the repository with statics and the repository with the generating script;
  2. Update the repository with statics using the generating script;
  3. Push changes of the repository with static to the main branch;
  4. Notify the owner (me) via Telegram.

Voilà! Now, whenever the repository with the original data changes, the GitHub immediately (well, as soon as possible — within a minute) updates the repository with the site and deploys it via GitHub Pages. A bonus is a web interface to manage the site (in fact, the GitHub site). No Code. :-)

While I'm at it, I added links for editing pages directly to the site (the pencil icon in the upper-right corner). This is intended as a convenience for me, but anyone who finds a typo can send a PR. Thank you in advance!

Hammer & Nails
15 September 2021 ·

I was developing payment documents in our configuration last week and came across an incredibly redundant solution to a primitive problem. Sorry, I can't keep to myself.

Just imagine: you have a document, which contains several tabular sections. Each of them has a comment field. You make a print form for this document; if at least one row of any TS contains a comment — you need to use one template 1, if there are no comments — template 2.

The task is pretty primitive, isn't it? All of us have done something like this a million times. Just read the selection, use IsBlankString() on the comment field and load the appropriate template. Coffee time!

However, instead of a short cycle, I saw this:

There is a chain of queries, in the lowest of which we scan all the TS (which, I remind you, we just raked out for printing). We are looking for comments in them, then we group the result several times and return it to the script.

Well, I'm not even talking about the load on the DBMS (I would venture to guess that this trick doesn't give a noticeable effect — after all, the selection is going to be small). It's just… Well… Checking a selection of rows is, like, five lines of code. Clear, simple, short, Sonar has no room to swear. How could you give birth to this? Because of great love for queries?

You know what? I bet that it's the correct answer. I can almost see this programmer, who has just mastered the query language more or less tolerably. He is in the absolute delight of new opportunities, so… If all you have is a hammer, everything around looks like nails.

No Comment
8 September 2021 ·

I did not notice when I gave up the habit of pedantically commenting on every method with which I have to work. This practice has some clever name for sure, but I don't care, to be honest. I mean the style when a description is added to every meaningful block of code, like this:

The meaning here is simple: when you dig in some dense legacy and run back and forth between chaotically scattered, big procedures — it is rather difficult to keep the logic of each of them in your head. The next cup of coffee will wash everything away. Therefore, such notes greatly speed up orientation on the ground, and the more time passes between approaches to the code, the more noticeable the effect.

However, at some point it became clear that this know-how is just a crutch supporting the frankly crappy code design. If you have a long procedure or function - take a breath, sit down and cut the fatty one into smaller methods. You will save both time and nerves, and you will figure out the code faster, and you will delight SonarCube.

A Slow Notification
18 August 2021 ·

This tweet reminded me of a job I once worked on. A client gets in touch: 1C is slow, do something. We ask a few questions. Okay, not all of 1C, just one operation.

They’re running a heavily rewritten Trade Management configuration, and the slow bit is custom code. Inside, it’s queries nested all over the place, a lot of messing about with value tables, some dubious calculations, and a bunch of server procedures seven hundred lines long each. We can’t copy the infobase, the technological log is unavailable, and DBMS and performance counter access are blocked. Debugging on the 1C server is off, and enabling it isn’t an option.

A mess. How can we find where it bogs down? Well, we can change the configuration; that’s something. I time the operation: yes, it thinks about something for a couple of minutes. Excellent! Rubbing my hands, I narrow the search by adding a whole pile of measurements to the most suspicious sections.

And here’s the funny part: nothing’s slow! The code doesn’t exactly fly, but we’re nowhere near minutes. For something this complicated, the timings look fine. Could it be serialization between client and server? I go through the server procedure carefully. Nope, nothing’s being passed back. Everything on the server stays there.

I move to the client code. What could possibly be slow here? Simplified, it looked something like this:

I stared at that code like an idiot for about ten minutes. Eventually, I asked a colleague, who told me something surprising: Notify() doesn’t just send notifications to every open form, it waits for their notification handlers to finish.

That blew my mind. I went digging and eventually found a form that caught the operation-completed event and immediately refreshed its dynamic lists. A query in one of those lists caused the delay: a subquery inside a subquery inside a subquery, plus a pile of joins “through a dot.” Nothing interesting after that.

Well, there you have it :-) Notify with care!

Finding Long Queries with Python
18 Jule 2021 ·

I’ve published a Python script for finding long-running queries in the 1C technological log. I wrote it in a fit of despair: I couldn’t understand why my trusty Bash script reported an average execution time higher than the maximum for one query.

The problem turned out to be gawk. With some log events, it couldn’t work out the duration: it tried to convert a string to a number, failed, and… Oh, no! Of course it didn’t throw an exception! It simply treated those strings as zero and calmly carried on.

The fix was even sillier than the problem: I simply added an explicit string-to-number conversion, and everything worked. How the hell is an explicit conversion different from an implicit one in gawk-land? And, more importantly, why?

Well, that was a circus. At least I got a new script out of it, and it goes easier on memory and CPU too. In the Bash version, I used three collections to calculate execution count, total execution time, and maximum execution time, each keyed by query text and context. All three had to be updated and kept in memory.

That works until you get into hundreds of thousands of entries. Then the collections start eating gigabytes of RAM, and searching them burns through CPU time. The new script is more straightforward: one collection stores all the data for each query.

Why Not Bash?
3 Jule 2021 ·

In my previous note, I discussed tasks where Bash is the perfect tool: minimal constraints and simple requirements. I also mentioned that sometimes it can’t cope at all.

Here’s one I actually ran into. Suppose we have around seventy gigabytes of 1C technological logs and need to rank exception descriptions from most to least frequent.

Easy, right? Extract EXCP, get Descr, count repetitions. I’d even written the necessary script before. I run it and patiently wait…

Know how long it took? Neither do I: after a day, I stopped it and investigated. Something was getting stuck inside gawk: it was hammering the CPU, with cat occasionally chipping in to read more data.

Well, crap. I thought about it and rewrote the script in Python. The new version finished in fifteen minutes and gave me:

  1. A ranking of exception descriptions;
  2. A script I can read six months later without Google;
  3. Confidence that I can add two or three conditions without accidentally summoning Satan through a combination of operators and flags.

Of course, I could have optimized the Bash version. The array lookups are probably what’s slow: the more descriptions you’ve collected, the longer each search takes, growing linearly with the array size. I could change the collection approach, using gawk only to extract descriptions and passing the results to sort and uniq.

But that starts to resemble the meme about a loaf of bread: you can build a trolleybus out of it, sure, but why? Come on, I just need to solve the problem. Python already did that with flying colors, saving me a lot of time and nerves.

That’s my point. We know Bash has its quirks, and often we can live with them. We know what it’s good at too. But sometimes the question becomes: is getting a solution specifically in Bash worth spending two hours wrestling with utilities, parameters, manuals, and Stack Overflow posts?

That’s why not Bash.

UPDATE: A good post by Ivan Grishaev on the same subject.

Why Bash?
23 June 2021 ·

I occasionally see colleagues asking: is 1C still messing around with Bash? Why not Python? Or PowerShell, at least? Weirdos!

Yes, Bash isn’t native to Windows, which is native territory for 1C, and getting it onto Windows is a job in itself. Yes, as a task grows more complicated, script readability drops exponentially. Yes, Bash simply can’t handle some tasks.

But its main advantage is that, for many 1C technological log analysis tasks, it is the simplest and fastest solution. Like an old screwdriver your grandfather used: always at hand, scratched, nicked, and a little awkward, but still working perfectly.

An example? Suppose we need to extract exceptions from the log. Let’s keep it simple and say we only need the first line of each event. We get something like this in Python.

You’ll say it can easily be cut in half, or even to a third. After all, it’s just a one-off job. Why fuss about readability and predictability?

Agreed! But let’s first solve the same task in Bash:

grep -r --include "*.log" ',EXCP,' > result.txt

That’s why Bash.

Metadata Not Found
8 June 2021 ·

I doubt many people have run into this one. First, you need to use the platform’s built-in data history, which isn’t especially popular. Some people are tied to the Standard Subsystems Library, which still uses familiar versioning through information registers; others don’t like how it’s implemented, and to be fair, the performance does have some rough edges.

Second, you need to disable data history for a metadata object and delete its accumulated object versions before new changes move from the buffer into the main table.

Here’s how data history works. It’s off by default. If you have the right permissions, you can turn it on for the objects you need: constants, catalogs, documents, and so on. The platform then records exactly what changes in those objects. It does this in two stages: first, a relatively fast write to an intermediate buffer, _DataHistoryQueue0; then, when UpdateHistory() is called, the data moves to the main version table, _DataHistoryVersions, and shows up in the app.

History can be updated immediately on writing, but to shorten the transaction, that step is usually moved into a scheduled job. So the data moves out of the buffer every so often, say once every five minutes. If, between an object’s data change and the history update, you disable its history and delete its versions, UpdateHistory() throws an exception: it tries to move changes from the buffer to the main table, but can’t match them up with the data already there.

Here’s some code that reproduces the problem with the Items catalog on platform 8.3.17.1989. Swap in any other object that supports data history; the result is the same.

How do you avoid the error? Obviously, call UpdateHistory() immediately before disabling history for the object. Ideally, do this when users aren’t working in the system: someone’s transaction could slip in between updating and disabling history and cause the same problem. Exclusive mode can guarantee that won’t happen.

An exclusive lock on the object’s table also comes to mind, but the documentation advises against calling UpdateHistory() inside transactions, so I’m not sure about that.

How do you fix the error? Enable data history for the affected object, update history, and disable it again. Back out, then try again properly, so to speak.

7 June 2021 ·

I posted on GitHub a Python script which I use to sync files between my PC and a NAS. I have a Synology DS220j; a lot of software comes with it, including a backup utility. However, it seems to have been made for show only: the program began to fail even at the setup stage, so I lost confidence in it pretty fast.

I suffered with the problem for some time and eventually returned to the good old rclone, which has only two problems for me. Firstly, I can't normally connect to an SMB share: yes, the login and password can be saved in Windows and rclone will use them, but OS will forget it as soon as possible. I got out of the situation by connecting my NAS as an external drive.

Secondly, I had many files and folders to sync: a directory here, a directory there, a config from there, a profile from here… In order not to produce spaghetti code, I wrote a simple script that takes sources and receivers from a config file, and then executes rclone for each pair.

Preparing for the 1C:Expert Exam
25 May 2021 ·

In mid-May, I passed the 1C Expert exam on the technical side of large implementations. I’d spent almost two years preparing, so I’m damn glad I finally got through it.

There’s tons of material online about the exam and everything around it, from Viktor Bogachev’s course to, say, a Telegram chat on the subject. So there’s no shortage of answers to the question in the title. But there are a couple of ways this can mess with your head that people rarely talk about. It helps to know about them beforehand.

Not Enough Dopamine

This exam is hard. Preparing can take a long time, and so can passing it: there’s a good chance you’ll need several attempts. I passed on my second try, but it varies. Some people I know passed on their third, fifth, or even eighth attempt.

You can end up putting in a huge effort again and again with nothing to show for it. Eventually, your brain decides this is something to avoid: it never works out, it feels pointless, and it makes you miserable. You can guess what that does to your chances of passing.

That’s why it’s better to treat preparation as a long, risky project: break it up with small tasks you can actually finish and feel good about. Your brain doesn’t draw much distinction between big and small successes, and getting back to the main project will be easier.

For example, as a distraction I wrote home automation scripts: the static site generator for this website, an organizer based on text files, tools for my home NAS, and other things I’d never got around to. Any tasks will do, including ones that have nothing to do with IT. Unclog the bathroom drain? Excellent idea!

Not Enough Memory

Unless you deal with 1C performance problems every day, this exam eats up a lot of mental RAM. You have to keep all sorts of things in your head that you’d normally just look up: Microsoft SQL Server trace flags and dynamic view names, PostgreSQL settings and recommended values, the platform’s standard indexes, and so on and so forth. A hu-u-uge pile of information! (gestures to show how huge)

Give your brain enough data, and it starts acting suspiciously like a DBMS with an overflowing buffer cache. In other words, anything you don’t need right now will be evicted from memory. Be prepared to forget the most unexpected things: your apartment number, the neighbor’s dog’s name, your wife’s birthday, and those aren’t even the strangest consequences. While preparing, I could really relate to Johnny Mnemonic, the guy from an ancient cyberpunk film who loaded so much data into his brain that he nearly died :-)

I see two ways out, both fairly obvious.

First, get some practice in. Complicated technical details are a hundred times easier to remember when they bring up a picture of the app where you tried them out.

Second, find something to associate the really tricky bits with. Take Bash! The utility name sed is easier to remember if you know it stands for Stream EDitor. The name cat comes from concatenate, not the animal, but if the animal helps you remember it, use that. Why not?

Or take the byte order mark: \xef\xbb\xbf, yes. I got it to stick with, don’t laugh, the completely unrelated phrase “Elf Friend BB Best Fight.” I have no idea why my brain needs such ass-backwards such roundabout ways of getting things in, but I’m not complaining. Whatever works!

A Bunch of Scripts

I’ve put a few more scripts on GitHub that I wrote recently to dig through the platform’s technological log:

  • Frequent Events. Groups events by name, counts occurrences, and lists them in descending order, from most to least frequent. Not sure this one is much use in practice; I just wanted to note down which cluster process writes which events.

The Date Literal Problem During Totals Recalculation
6 February 2021 ·

So, during a routine totals recalculation from the Configurator, we suddenly got the error: "the year in the Date literal exceeds 3999". Which means there's a date somewhere in the database — or trying to get there — that is beyond the maximum 1C can handle: 31.12.3999 23:59:59.

Alright. What do we do with that?

The main thing is to identify the exact table that contains the bad dates. Since the error showed up during totals recalculation, the obvious place to look is the registers. Open the standard totals management tool, start recalculation, and you'll get the name of the register the platform trips over.

Another approach — more proper, methodologically speaking — is to enable tech log collection (SDBL, EXCP, and EXCPCNTX) and get a log that looks roughly like this. In that log, find the EXCP event, and right before it the SDBL event. That SDBL entry contains the SQL query that caused the crash. In its text, you'll see the table name you need (AccumRgTn11530). The corresponding configuration object name can be pulled out with pretty much any utility built around GetDBStorageStructureInfo().

One way or another, you end up with the register name. Open its form, sort by period, and you'll quickly get to the bad entries. Then the job is to inspect the documents that created those records, fix the root cause, and repost the documents. If totals recalculation is still broken after that, then either this is not the only table with broken dates, or those dates have already spread somewhere beyond the records table.

For example, I once had a case where fixing the records was not enough, because records with invalid dates were still sitting in the turnover table. The platform itself could not remove them, but the database was small enough that I could get away with some restructuring tricks. I pulled the following stunt: turned off the "Use in totals" flag for all register dimensions and applied the changes; then turned it back on and recalculated totals again. As a result, the register's turnover table was physically dropped, then recreated and filled from scratch — this time without dates from the distant future.

As a last resort, you could delete the bad records with direct SQL queries (DELETE or even TRUNCATE). But first, that violates the platform vendor's license agreement, and second, it's risky: it's very easy to remove something important and not notice until later. So I would, uh, not recommend trying that at home.

the main thing is to identify the exact table that contains the bad dates. since the error showed up during totals recalculation, the obvious place to look is the registers. open the standard totals management tool, start recalculation, and you'll get the name of the register the platform trips over. another approach — more proper, methodologically speaking — is to enable tech log collection ( sdbl , excp , and excpcntx ) and get a log that looks roughly like this . in that log, find the excp event, and right before it the sdbl event. that sdbl entry contains the sql query that caused the crash. in its text, you'll see the table name you need ( accumrgtn11530 ). the corresponding configuration object name can be pulled out with pretty much any utility built around getdbstoragestructureinfo() . one way or another, you end up with the register name. open its form, sort by period, and you'll quickly get to the bad entries . then the job is to inspect the documents that created those records, fix the root cause, and repost the documents. if totals recalculation is still broken after that, then either this is not the only table with broken dates, or those dates have already spread somewhere beyond the records table. for example, i once had a case where fixing the records was not enough, because records with invalid dates were still sitting in the turnover table. the platform itself could not remove them, but the database was small enough that i could get away with some restructuring tricks. i pulled the following stunt: turned off the "use in totals" flag for all register dimensions and applied the changes; then turned it back on and recalculated totals again. as a result, the register's turnover table was physically dropped, then recreated and filled from scratch — this time without dates from the distant future. as a last resort, you could delete the bad records with direct sql queries ( delete or even truncate ). but first, that violates the platform vendor's license agreement, and second, it's risky: it's very easy to remove something important and not notice until later. so i would, uh, not recommend trying that at home.

Checking an Object’s Visibility
17 January 2021 ·

The platform has a few different ways to decide whether a user can see a metadata object. One is functional options. If you haven’t used them before, here’s the short version: an object can be included in an option that is either active in a particular infobase, making it visible to users, or inactive, hiding it. An object can belong to several options, in which case it appears if at least one is active, or to none, in which case users always see it.

I remember looking, about five years ago, for a way to tell from code whether a user could see an object, just as far as functional options are concerned. For some reason, I didn’t find a solution then, although it’s ridiculously simple. Here’s a function for exactly that. The logic:

  1. Iterate through the options and look for the object in each one.
  2. If the object belongs to an option, check whether that option is active. If so, the user can see the object.
  3. If the object belongs to no options, the user can see it too.

You’d want to cache the result, of course, if only because there’s a query inside a loop. Apart from that, it does the job. I still can’t understand why I didn’t write something similar back then. Man, I hope that five years from now, the things driving me nuts today will look just as easy to fix.

Searching Files Recursively
14 January 2021 ·

Some time ago, I tried finding code vulnerabilities with Bash scripts. Sounds intimidating, but it’s just recursive text searching with regular expressions. I wrote the scripts, but as I realized today, I did it in a rather… ass-backwards way, ahem. All you need is egrep! Out of find, xargs, and egrep, we can throw away two of the three.

For example, today our configuration stopped building in the latest EDT release. We suspected broken GUIDs: references to metadata objects removed from the configuration. The platform doesn’t always clean these up after deleting the objects themselves. I’ve written about this a couple of times, for example here and here.

We decided to search the configuration export for GUIDs and check whether they all belonged where they were. All it takes is one command:

egrep -rn '.{8}-.{4}-.{4}-.{4}-.{12}' dump

The r flag enables recursive search; n adds not only the filename but also the line number to each match. The final parameter, dump, is the directory to search.

You could make the regex more precise, but this is plenty. False positives, GUIDs that aren’t broken references, are easy to filter through a pipe. For example, the following script excludes GUID-containing lines that include “uuid”:

egrep -rn '.{8}-.{4}-.{4}-.{4}-.{12}' dump | grep -v 'uuid'

html:
Good Old DATETIME
11 November 2020 ·

I did some reading online about date types in MS SQL Server, and I no longer wonder why 1C still clings to its date offset. People describe a whole bundle of DATETIME2 problems:

  1. You can’t do basic date arithmetic. Want to subtract two dates or add a day? You’ll need a workaround.
  2. Standard functions still return good old DATETIME, DATEADD for example. If you store your data as DATETIME2, you have to convert it.
  3. Fields of this type don’t index well, since each DATETIME2 value is stored backwards, time first, date second. So the DBMS gets its row count estimate wrong and comes up with a bad execution plan.

You can read more on Towards Data Science or, for example, SQL Server Central.

html:
Date Offsets in 1C
10 November 2020 ·

MS SQL Server DATETIME fields cannot store dates before 1753. Try writing January 1, 0001 to the database, for example, and you’ll get an out-of-range value error. I thought this was a funny old quirk for such a well-established DBMS until I stumbled across the reason.

Briefly, Britain adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1752, losing eleven days in the process. That created a problem: suppose a user wants the difference in days between 1653 and 1753. What should happen? Account for the missing days? Ignore them? Add hints or settings?

Apparently, the developers decided not to get into all that and just cut off the date range. If you need earlier dates, DATETIME2 doesn’t have that restriction.

As for 1C, the platform originally used DATETIME and devised a special workaround to avoid trouble storing dates before 1753. In short, when writing dates to the database, it quietly adds two thousand years to each one, then subtracts them when reading. A user sees January 1, 2000 in 1C, while the database actually stores January 1, 4000.

I wonder why 1C hasn’t thrown this out yet. The platform uses DATETIME2 now, so it shouldn’t need the offset trick anymore. Maybe there’s a catch, or maybe they’re just being careful, but the DBMS developers themselves seem quite confident:

Your great great great great great great great grandfather should upgrade to SQL Server 2008 and use the DateTime2 data type, which supports dates in the range: 0001-01-01 through 9999-12-31.

Joe Stefanelli (SQL Server developer)

Perhaps it’s simply at the bottom of the priority list. Adding and subtracting two thousand years for every date increases hardware load, of course, but it gets lost among everything else.

html:
Hulk Delete!
9 November 2020 ·

On a PostgreSQL course, I learned a funny detail: in version 10, the DBMS developers renamed pg_xlog, containing write-ahead logs, to pg_wal, and pg_clog, containing transaction statuses, to pg_xact.

Know why? Because of admins with more confidence than experience, who saw “log” in a folder name and went for it. I need to free some disk space, they’d think, and this DBMS has filled it all with stupid logs. No time to investigate: rm -rf the lot, problem solved!

So out went both the protection for data operations in the buffer cache and multiversion concurrency control, in one fell swoop. The cluster then died in agony. There was plenty of free disk space, but I’m afraid the joy didn’t last long :-)

Investigating an Error in Designer
31 October 2020 ·

So, Designer reports an error, and we need to fix it or find a workaround. This could get awkward: we can’t look at the application’s code. Still, to fix it, we need to work out what Designer was doing before it fell over, and why it couldn’t finish.

What can help?

First, the error message itself. Often, that alone is enough to get your thoughts moving in the right direction. If a query caused the failure, the error will also include a message from the DBMS.

Second, the technological log, capturing EXCP, SDBL, and DBMSSQL (DBPOSTGRS?) events for t:applicationName=Designer. That shows us the exceptions inside Designer and the queries it runs, which are often what went wrong.

A database query trace can also help. With MS SQL, you can capture it using Extended Events; specifically, we’re interested in error_reported, rpc_completed, and sql_batch_completed. The principle is the same: capture query execution errors and the queries themselves.

Here’s an example. Maybe not the best one, but it’s fresh.

We’re working with a configuration that uses data separation. Its database is divided into pieces, or data areas, each of which knows nothing about its neighbors: how many there are, their sizes, and so forth. The database also contains shared data, such as catalogs accessible from any area. These usually hold technical information, for example a list of metadata objects.

We need to take the FileStorageVolumes catalog out of the main separator. The catalog is currently separated, meaning its data differs from one area to another. We need its contents to become the same across all areas.

This should be straightforward, since the catalog table is empty: no area stores anything in it. We apply the setting, and:

The exception text contains two messages: one from the platform, the other from the DBMS. The first one makes me scratch my head: what does it mean, the data isn’t unique? The catalog is empty; there’s no data. Maybe something’s wrong with one of the supporting structures, rather than the catalog data itself.

The DBMS message is clearer: MS SQL Server tried to create a unique index on _DataHistorySettingsNG, but couldn’t because combinations of indexed fields weren’t unique. It even gives the specific value that prevented index creation: NULL.

Conclusions?

  1. The problem clearly arose during restructuring. First, that’s exactly what we were doing. Second, both CREATE UNIQUE INDEX, since creating indexes is part of restructuring, and the problematic table’s name point to it. The NG suffix is assigned to table copies created during restructuring. If restructuring succeeds, the platform drops the original table and renames the copy.
  2. The problem involves the data history mechanism’s settings, _DataHistorySettings. This table stores each metadata object’s status: whether to maintain data history for the object, its fields, and its tabular section fields, if any.

That explains how an empty catalog can have a uniqueness problem: an object’s data history settings exist independently of whether the object contains data. The settings table has just three fields: _MetadataId (the metadata object’s ID), _Content (setting values), and _Fld626 (the area separator).

Before restructuring, the data looks roughly like this:

But then the picture changed. When we excluded the catalog from the common attribute, Designer started restructuring: it created _DataHistorySettingsNG, copied the data from _DataHistorySettings, and set _Fld626 to NULL for all records belonging to FileStorageVolumes.

The result? A whole pile of settings for FileStorageVolumes that belong to no data area. That sounds unhealthy in itself, but the real trouble started when Designer tried to create the table’s clustered index. It is built on _MetadataId and _Fld626 and is unique, so it cannot be created: many records differ only in _Content, while _MetadataId and _Fld626 are guaranteed to be identical.

Just to be sure, let’s check the technological log. I’ve stripped out the unrelated events and other clutter. Sure enough: Designer creates and populates _DataHistorySettingsNG, tries to index it, receives an error, and drops it. The DBMS trace shows roughly the same picture.

That’s where the interesting part ends, since the solution is fairly obvious: delete the catalog’s data history settings in every data area and repeat restructuring. This doesn’t fix the bug, of course. Really, Designer should catch this and give us a sensible error message, as it does when deleting an information register dimension would violate the uniqueness of its records. But it does get the task done.

And we’re done. Look at us go!

Counting Exceptions in the Technological Log
24 October 2020 ·

Another script. It counts exceptions per minute and ranks the results, so you can quickly see when the applications were having a particularly bad time.

Along the way, two odd little problems threw me off. First, for some reason I was convinced that uniq -c groups lines regardless of where they occur in the data stream. Take this:

банан
банан
груша
банан

I thought that feeding this data to uniq -c would group identical lines, count repetitions, and produce something like this:

3 банан
1 груша

But what I actually got was:

2 банан
1 груша
1 банан

Turns out uniq expects repeated lines to sit next to each other. If a line differs from the previous one, it starts a new count for that line. To get the result I expected, you have to sort the data first, then pass it to uniq.

The second problem involved sed. I was trying to use it to remove everything from the data stream except hours and minutes; the attempt is on line 12 of the script. But some events stubbornly failed to match the regular expression despite looking exactly the same. I wasted a lot of time and got thoroughly annoyed before remembering BOM. Once I removed the markers, everything went smoothly.

Every technological log file uses a BOM, which you can confirm with this script, for example. Each log begins with special characters invisible to the naked eye, and these can prevent the first line from being processed because they don’t match the regular expression.

My takeaway is to strip BOMs out by default, rather than wonder every time whether they’ll cause trouble. Sometimes this will be unnecessary; a BOM doesn’t interfere with solving the task above using grep, for instance. But I don’t like surprises. Besides, a few processor cycles spent on a simple replacement are a much better deal than the equivalent in fried nerves and wasted time.

Queries and Lock Waits
19 October 2020 ·

I’ve put together two more technological log analysis scripts: the first ranks heavy MS SQL queries, and the second ranks long lock waits.

I pick out heavy queries by how long their DBMSSQL events lasted. The longer a query takes, the more likely it is to have eaten a lot of resources. That usually holds up, though you’d need a trace to diagnose it properly.

Lock waits are also measured by duration. The script also checks that the TLOCK event has something in WaitConnections. That tells us the platform really was waiting to get a lock, rather than just taking a while to set one.

An Updated Top Exceptions Script
17 October 2020 ·

I rewrote the Bash script that ranks exceptions in a collected technological log: I wanted a simpler way to do it.

Out went all the fiddling with replacing event beginnings with a gawk record separator: you can just give gawk a regex for that. I also moved more of the logic into gawk itself. It’s easier to follow, especially if I want to add to it later.

It’s clearly better than before, or at least the logic is easier to understand. Originally, though, I wanted to make the script smaller and get something like this:

grep -hoP ",EXCP,.*\KDescr=.*" */*.log | uniq -c | sort -rn

Filter only lines with EXCP events, cut everything before the error description, and group with uniq. Very elegant, I think.

Except EXCP descriptions can run over several lines. So sometimes we’d lose information we need to figure out what happened: everything after the first line break. I haven’t yet worked out how to solve that without tripling the script’s size :-)

html:
Vulnerabilities in 1C Configurations
13 October 2020 ·

Last month, I attended an Infostart meetup about security in 1C-based solutions. I learned a lot! Among other things, Oleg Tymko talked about things we do in code that can leave a product vulnerable: hard-coded IP addresses, links, email addresses, passwords, that sort of thing.

Yesterday, I put together a simple Bash script that searches a configuration export for such issues. Essentially, it just runs regular expressions over the configuration. I didn’t put too much thought into it, just tried a couple of approaches for the fun of it.

My takeaway? If you’re going to keep developing this seriously, start with something like SonarQube. Brute-force approaches produce too many false positives; you need filters, exceptions, history, and supporting infrastructure.

For a quick look, though, this does the job: no infrastructure, no fussing with configuration or hardware. Export the configuration, kick Bash into action, and that’s it: results in a few seconds.

On Single Sign-On
12 September 2020 ·

Whatever else you make of this clash of two yokozuna the Apple–Epic Games fight, it’s a great reminder that you shouldn’t use Single Sign-On on the internet: anywhere, ever, on any service. Who knows which giants will suddenly come to blows next, or which website will ban you for no clear reason? Because screw you, dude, that’s why.

The users in that tweet might get off lightly. But if, say, Google blocks your account, you could be in real trouble: a pile of services you accessed through Google will suddenly turn into pumpkins.

There are plenty of solutions just as convenient as Single Sign-On. Password managers, browser extensions, hardware keys: almost anything is better than proprietary, closed-source services you have no say in.

Unresolved References to Functional Options
19 August 2020 ·

Here’s one way to solve unresolved references left after deleting a functional option. It starts with a configuration check giving me a couple of dozen messages like this:

CommonForm.PersonalSettings.Form Unresolved metadata object references (2)
Catalog.BankAccounts.Form.GLAccountsEditForm.Form Unresolved metadata object references (1)
Catalog.CashRegisters.Form.GLAccountsEditForm.Form Unresolved metadata object references (1)

I export the configuration to files and open Form.xml for one of the affected forms. I pick a form with fewer controls, so there’s less stuff to sift through.

A quick scan for anything unusual doesn’t take long:

A normal functional option reference is its name, as with DepreciationOfAssets. If there’s a GUID instead, that functional option is missing from the configuration. The reference is unresolved.

I search the rest of the export for that GUID, and there are almost all the problems the platform complained about. Fixing them is easy: remove the broken reference from the XML and load the file back into the configuration. There’s an even simpler approach: open the form control’s functional options list and immediately save it. That also removes the broken reference.

Why is looking for these strays in Designer itself a job for incurable optimists? Because the problem is almost impossible to notice. At best, you’ll see something like this:

Designer knows there are two options in the field, but can’t get a name for the second one. It’s gone. And most often there’s only one functional option! Then it looks like this:

html:
A Method with a Surprise
27 Jule 2020 ·

A couple of weeks ago, I encountered an annoying bug. The task couldn’t be simpler: find a document by number. Do it this way, and the document is found:

SELECT Ref FROM Document.Invoice WHERE Number = &Number

But this way? No luck:

Documents.Invoice.FindByNumber(Number)

At first I froze for a moment, then checked the documentation and, of course, found the answer. FindByNumber() has a second parameter, IntervalDate, for finding documents with periodic numbering. It narrows the search to a particular period. If numbering resets annually and you pass May 1, 2020, for example, the search covers January 1 through December 31, 2020. And Invoice does indeed use annual numbering.

So what’s the problem? The vague phrase “the parameter is used for documents with periodic numbering” actually hides an iron rule: you cannot omit the parameter for such documents.

To check, let’s look at the SQL the DBMS actually runs. An ordinary query brings no surprises. P1 is the separator, P2 the document number:

SELECT
    T1._IDRRef 
FROM
    dbo._Document283 T1
WHERE
    ((T1._Fld704 = @P1))
    AND ((T1._Number = @P2))

But calling FindByNumber() adds a third parameter with the value 2001-12-31 23:59:59. Yes, “the end of the first year since the beginning of time”:

SELECT
    T1._IDRRef
FROM
    dbo._Document283 T1
WHERE
    ((T1._Fld704 = @P1))
    AND
    (
        T1._Number = @P2
        AND T1._Date_Time <= @P3
    )

Naturally, this query doesn’t find the required document. It won’t find anything in a real infobase, ever, under any circumstances.

The solution is clear: pass IntervalDate or, if we don’t have a date, use the Standard Subsystems Library’s ObjectAttributeValue() or an equivalent. But honestly, the platform should throw an exception when FindByNumber() is called without IntervalDate on a document with periodic numbering, rather than quietly execute a query guaranteed to be pointless.

One Query to Rule Them All
25 Jule 2020 ·

For posterity, I’ve uploaded one of the inefficient queries I worked on a few months ago to GitHub Gist. It powered a dynamic list on a catalog item form, and whenever the user opened that tab, the platform went off to meditate, even with a relatively small database.

At first glance, it looks straightforward: a bunch of queries against document tables, joined with UNION ALL. Each table is filtered by roughly the same conditions: reference type, date, and whether the reference appears in a subquery’s result.

But there are several potential problems. First, at least 14 tables are involved, one per combined query. That alone raises the risk that the optimizer won’t have time to choose even a reasonably decent plan. Most likely, it will just take a wild guess and hope for the best.

Second, much of that work is probably wasted. Each query has something like this:

WHERE VALUETYPE(AdditionalExpenses.Ref) IN (&DocumentsListSelectedTypes)

The dynamic list receives a list of document types to display. But that filter kicks in after the data has been read: even if the user only wants invoices, the DBMS still reads all 14 tables, then discards 13 of them.

Still, none of that is especially critical. If that were the full list of problems, we might never have investigated. The main issue is the second condition in the WHERE clauses: each query checks whether the document reference appears in a subquery’s result.

Using subqueries in conditions is almost taboo unless temporary tables are involved: the DBMS often can’t work out how much data it’ll get back, or how best to handle it. And the data source makes things even worse here. A filter criterion isn’t a database table you can read, even by scanning; it’s a collection of tables. DocumentsByProject contains thirty!

That sounds bad enough, but there’s more: each of the fourteen combined queries selects documents of a particular type from those thirty tables.

And… scene :-)

A Blog in Vue.js
21 Jule 2020 ·

In the middle of last year, I got excited about rewriting this website with something more modern than PHP, chose Vue.js as the framework, and got to work. I barely knew JavaScript at the time, so I stumbled over plenty of things like “the date formatting method crashes in Safari.” Eventually, though, I had a working app.

Well, sort of. On one hand, I achieved my main goal: a client-side web application that only asks the server for data and builds the entire interface itself. On the other, I had to bolt an army of workarounds hooks onto the framework even for basic things, like highlighting menu items or returning the correct HTTP codes. Some things I couldn’t get working at all on the first go, such as serving HTML versions of pages to Yandex, whose crawlers in 2020 can’t index JavaScript websites.

I learned a lot, but the end result was such a mixed bag that I eventually gave up on the idea and published the resulting Frankenstein on GitHub. Perhaps it will save someone time on tasks like “display arbitrary HTML through Vue.js” or “make VueI18n work with Russian.”

There’s no documentation, though. I initially wanted to explain how everything worked, but quickly realized it would take a lot of time for little obvious benefit. I’ll probably return to the subject when the mood strikes. For now, let’s call it an MVP :-)

The Size of Data in a 1C Database
11 Jule 2020 ·

Last week, while browsing the 8.3.15 release notes, I came across GetDatabaseDataSize(). I got curious about how it works and how its numbers compare with what you get from, say, Management Studio.

I ended up writing a sort of console to pass various metadata objects to the method, and started watching the platform’s database queries.

Basically, the platform works out the data size with something like this:

CAST(
    SUM(
        CAST(
            DATALENGTH(T1._Fld40) AS NUMERIC(12, 0)
        )
    ) AS NUMERIC(18, 0)
)

It does this for every field in the object, including standard attributes. If there are tabular sections, it counts those too, then sums the results.

Conclusions?

First, now I understand the method’s awkward name. It doesn’t calculate table size, as I initially thought, but data size specifically. The estimate excludes schema overhead, index overhead, and extent allocation. It counts only the size of the data stored directly in the object.

So a product catalog, say, will actually take up more space than this method reports. Possibly a lot more. You wouldn’t use it for precise analysis, but it’s fine for a quick look at where the data is piling up.

Second, the method doesn’t count the data history overhead for the objects being analyzed, which the docs are quite clear about. In theory, you could calculate it manually starting from _DataHistoryMetadata, but let’s wait a release or two: perhaps the developers will add it.

Third, the DBMS reads all the data in the tables it needs, then works out how big that data is. That probably means a whole bunch of scans, which can flush the buffer cache pretty quickly. In 1cFresh, the queries respect data separators, but that’s cold comfort to me.

Use it with care on a live production system.

Exporting Standard Data Processors
5 Jule 2020 ·

We recently swapped out SSLi’s creaky old homegrown versioning for the platform’s built-in data history in our configuration. I’m now finishing data history backup and restore. Surprisingly, neither the Standard Subsystems Library, the Standard Technologies Library, nor SSLi can do this yet, though I didn’t expect it from the last one.

I’ll write more when it’s finished. For now, here’s a neat trick that came in handy: the platform’s built-in data processors available through “All Functions” can be exported as ordinary epf files! Colleagues on Infostart explained the trick in detail here and here. In brief, the magic looks like this:

КопироватьФайл(
    "v8res://mngbase/StandardDataChangeHistory.epf",
    "Q:/StandardDataChangeHistory.epf"
);

The links above have the full list of forms and processors you can pull out, how to get that list, and plenty of people arguing about it all.

Why might this help you? Honestly, I don’t know. In our case, we were building interfaces for data history and were curious about how 1C had written its own. Spoiler: it’s pretty messy.

html:
On Perfect Balance
20 May 2020 ·

I want to share a couple of great pieces about modern software. Neither is exactly new, especially the first, but I’m sure some of you haven’t seen them:

  • Software Disenchantment by Nikita Tonsky
  • Everything in Software Is Amazing, but Nobody Is Happy by Evgeny Trifonov

What brought this to mind? Last week, I took part in a hackathon for developers at our company. I learned a lot of cool things and even shared first place with two other people who came up with very similar solutions.

(If you also work at First BIT, the results are on the portal, along with a review by another winner, Dima Leshchenko.)

Along the way, we had to deploy and configure a mountain of software: EDT, RabbitMQ, Docker, GitLab, JIRA, SonarQube, and a wagonload of smaller, simpler tools. All right, no complaints about RabbitMQ: it’s light and fast. But the rest… I already knew EDT had an appetite, but GitLab and JIRA’s hunger really surprised me.

Yes, everything ran in Docker; yes, the configuration wasn’t optimal, with several PostgreSQL servers instead of one, for example; yes, it was Docker for Windows, which every sysadmin I know loves to make jokes about. But twelve gigabytes of RAM straight out of the gate?! I won’t even mention the CPU: the load looked as if the computer were simulating a nuclear explosion in real time.

It’s hard to find a better illustration of Nikita’s points: this software devoured a sea of resources and calmly asked for more before it had even started doing anything useful. But Evgeny has a point too: with one single command, I got several operating systems up and running, complete with some pretty complicated servers. And it took a tiny fraction of the time it would have a few years ago.

I don’t have an answer. I don’t think anyone does. We’ve been having this argument forever. Pick either side, and you still end up trying to find a balance. You need to write good, fast code, while also avoiding premature optimization. Getting the code right feels great: you remember that, damn it, you’re pretty good! The second simply keeps you from losing your mind in search of the perfect bubble sort algorithm :-)

Managing Services with PowerShell
28 April 2020 ·

The other day, I sketched out a few PowerShell scripts for starting and stopping services on my work PC. I didn’t end up needing them, so I’ll leave a couple of examples here before I lose them:

get-service -Name 1C:Enterprise* | Where-Object {$_.status -eq 'running'} | stop-service -pass
get-service -Name *SQL* | Where-Object {$_.status -eq 'running'} | stop-service -pass

Both lines above do the same thing: find services with a particular name, check their status, and stop them if they’re running. Patterns come in handy for the service names. Microsoft SQL Server, for example, has a whole brood of services with different purposes, and it’s handy to kill them with one line. Or take the 1C:Enterprise server service: there’s only one, but its name is so long that I can’t be bothered to type it in full :-)

You can do pretty much the same thing with regular processes. This line looks for obs64 and stops it if it’s there.

get-process -Name obs64 | stop-process -pass

If you want the details, there’s plenty of documentation, packed with examples and discussions along the lines of “how to start a service while meditating on one leg in artificial zero gravity.”

IsEmpty() or ValueIsFilled()?
11 April 2020 ·

A few days ago, a colleague and I discussed the best way to check whether a reference is filled. I remembered an instructor telling us, very confidently, to be careful with ValueIsFilled(). Supposedly, it compares the variable with every possible empty value in the configuration, and the whole thing is a huge, slow mess. As an alternative, the instructor recommended the reference’s IsEmpty() method and checking composite attributes roughly like this:

СсылкаЗаполнена = Ссылка <> Неопределено И Не Ссылка.Пустая();

My colleague argued that ValueIsFilled() is faster because it’s a built-in function and doesn’t spend time looking up a method on an object, a relatively slow operation in scripting languages.

I can’t recall either method ever being a bottleneck, but I got curious and wrote a test that checks a reference variable for an empty value both ways and measures the time taken.

The average result looks roughly like this. There are four steps: the first two assume the reference is defined, while the third and fourth add a check for that. The table’s last column shows the execution context, client or server.

The result is pretty clear: ValueIsFilled() doesn’t slow things down at all. It’s actually faster than IsEmpty(), especially once we start checking the variable for Undefined. The difference isn’t enormous, of course, but it could save a couple of seconds in some lengthy scheduled operations.

Besides, one check that works for everything is easier than trying to guess every value the variable might have.

Recording Video
3 April 2020 ·

I work remotely, so I talk to colleagues over Zoom and Slack. Mostly in chats, but many subjects are still easier to discuss by voice. That’s where it gets awkward: forget message indexing and search, and, most importantly, there’s no conversation archive. Sometimes you really need to remember: who said it? What exactly? When?

Zoom and Slack don’t solve this on their own. Zoom only records meetings you organize or have permission to record, which is far from all of them, while Slack doesn’t record video at all.

Solving the Problem

I solved it some time ago by installing OBS Studio, screen recording software popular with streamers. It handles conference recording beautifully. Setup is minimal: record the entire screen, microphone audio, and all playback audio. After a few test recordings, you can add mixer filters such as gain and noise suppression.

Choose where to save the recordings under Output → Recording → Recording Path. We’re recording calls, so there’ll be lots of files. Might as well sort them into folders by day from the start. Go to Advanced settings and set Filename Formatting to something like %CCYY-%MM-%DD/%hh-%mm-%ss.

Quick Recording Controls

Opening OBS for every call is inconvenient, but it supports plenty of hotkeys. You can press some elaborate combination at the start and end of a conversation. That didn’t work for me, though: for some reason, the shortcuts kept slipping my mind. Even sticky notes didn’t help.

At first I got quite annoyed, then realized: if I can’t remember a shortcut, I should get rid of it. Start recording with one button, stop with another.

The hardware was easy: I have an ergonomic Microsoft keyboard with a wagonload of programmable buttons. Software was harder: OBS Studio understands some launch parameters, but there’s not much to choose from. There isn’t even a stop-recording option. I wanted more.

I eventually solved it with an OBS Studio plugin that lets you control a running instance. It was designed for remote recording control, from a smartphone for example, but it works just as well on the same machine.

Here’s what I ended up with:

  1. Install OBS Studio and the obs-websocket plugin. Clear “Enable System Tray Alerts” under Tools → WebSockets Server Settings, or it will report every little thing.
  2. Put this utility somewhere convenient to control the plugin from the command line.
  3. Assign OBSCommand.exe /startrecording to one button and OBSCommand.exe /stoprecording to another.
  4. Done. Look at you go!

A console window pops up for a moment when you press the button: OBSCommand launches, contacts obs-websocket, and waits for a reply. I initially wanted to hide the window, but changed my mind. If OBS Studio isn’t running or something goes wrong, the console will stay open, and at least I’ll know recording hasn’t started.

Unresolved References
10 Marth 2020 ·

Unresolved references to metadata objects usually appear when objects are deleted, and sometimes when configurations are merged. ITS has an article with a good explanation of the details.

Broken references don’t always affect the application’s behavior. A field without a data binding is easy to notice, of course. But suppose you delete a functional option: what does it matter if a reference remains somewhere in a form command? It simply sits there like a cut wire, inert and harmless. Nothing passes through it.

Still, these things gradually clutter the configuration and should be removed. The ITS advice isn’t all that helpful: go through every place a broken reference might be hiding. Imagine a complicated document form with lots of controls. How long would that search take? And success isn’t guaranteed.

There’s a rougher way that works: delete groups of controls from the form, one after another. Start with large groups, such as pages. After each removal, check the configuration and see whether the broken reference has disappeared. Before starting, it’s best to delete all form code so the platform doesn’t complain about references to nonexistent controls.

The problem might also be in the form itself rather than its controls, but that’s much easier to locate: settings storage, conditional appearance, commands. There aren’t many candidates.

You can also export the configuration to files and dig through the XML. That’s also worth doing because what you see in Designer can be misleading. If a form command references a missing functional option, for example, you might see nothing wrong in the command’s properties. But the XML will contain a suspicious GUID instead of an option name: practically a signed confession :-)

Filtering Standard Attributes
9 Marth 2020 ·

A short code fragment from the data history settings processor I just wrote about. It checks whether Attribute is MetadataObject’s standard attribute named StandardAttributeName. When is that useful? Suppose you’re iterating over an object’s standard attributes and want to skip one for some reason.

At first glance, the solution looks absurdly convoluted. Why not simply compare the attribute being checked with the one we want to exclude?

If Attribute = MetadataObject.StandardAttributes.Order Then

Because that code doesn’t work: comparing two standard attributes of a metadata object in the 1C platform always returns False.

All right, you might say, why complicate things? How about this?

If Attribute.Name = "Order" Then

That won’t work either if your code runs in a Russian configuration: the standard attribute we’re looking for is then named “Порядок.”

But you can look up the standard attribute in the collection by either its Russian or English name. Then you get its actual name and compare that with the name of the attribute you’re checking.

Of course, we could simply compare the name with both “Order” and “Порядок.” But first, that’s ugly; second, our coding standards don’t allow Russian in the code. I wanted a more general solution.

The Try/Catch is there in case the configuration has no standard attribute with that name at all. Trying to look it up would throw an error.

Data History Settings
9 Marth 2020 ·

I’ve put a data processor on GitHub for setting up the data history feature that arrived in the platform not long ago. Here’s what it does:

  1. Builds a tree of objects that support data history;
  2. Shows which objects currently have data history enabled;
  3. Lets you enable or disable data history for objects and their attributes.

It supports batch operations: for example, you can enable history for several documents and all catalogs at once. Or wipe all your changes and go back to the defaults the configuration developer set.

I think it turned out well. I mostly wrote it for myself, to give my brain a workout in the evenings, but we might even include it in our configuration! Right now, SSLi handles our data versioning, and it’s not exactly efficient: it’s slow and makes the database balloon. Hopefully, the platform will do better when we test it.

You can find similar tools on Infostart and ITS, but they’re either buggy, work only with Russian configurations (no English interface and dependencies on the Russian Standard Subsystems Library), or are just out of date, with no support for constants, for example.

The Ninth Wave
9 Marth 2020 ·

Yesterday morning, I was buying gifts for my women. While a florist was makings bouquets for me, we had a small talk and I suddenly caught her eye. She was looking at the growing crowd of customers with calmness and a clearly readable shadow of doom. This is probably how sailors looking at a surging wave which is about to bury their boat :-)

People outside the flower industry grin sometimes — they say, eight of March is such a magical holiday for all the florists who make a fortune in ten hours. Well, income is really good these days, but literally anybody who has ever worked in this sphere more often associates the holiday (and a couple of days before it, by the way) with a monstrous strain on health and nerves.

I can say that I got off cheaply: was just deploying and servicing some IT of a local net of flower shops, nothing more (by the way, I want to proudly recommend my former colleagues!). Nonetheless, the smell of flowers caused me Vietnam syndrome for a long time :-)

Top Exceptions in the Technological Log
16 February 2020 ·

I’ve published a Bash script on GitHub that identifies the most frequent exceptions in a collected 1C technological log.

It analyzes EXCP events. These are the main source of error information, though certainly not the only one: EXCPCNTX, for example, describes an event that had started but hadn’t finished when an error occurred. Also, if an exception occurs during a server call, the CALL event’s RetExcp field contains the error text returned to the client.

Most of the time, though, EXCP and the occasional EXCPCNTX will do. People often collect them by default: it doesn’t put any real load on the system and lets you run the logs through an analysis tool, such as the script above, to keep a finger on the pulse.

Debugging over HTTP
26 January 2020 ·

At the end of the week, I ran into a rather silly situation: TCP/IP debugging on a 1C server stopped working. Debug mode itself was enabled, but Designer couldn’t “see” the server’s debug contexts.

The silly part is how hard it is to find the cause: the platform gives you no clear error to work with. After checking the obvious possibilities, such as the firewall and ports, all you can do is shrug.

I solved it by switching to HTTP debugging. The overall setup is more complicated, but configuring it is quite simple. Briefly, you need to:

  • Start the server agent service with the “-debug -http” flags.
  • In Designer’s debugging settings (Tools → Options → Debug), select HTTP as the debugging protocol and the cluster debug server as the debug server.

There’s a more detailed walkthrough on ITS.

Unmaintainable Code
18 January 2020 ·

I happened across an example of a 1C query that calculates the difference between two dates in years, months, and days.

The code may work, I haven’t checked, but to me it’s a good example of what not to do. The problem is that its author will forget what most of those if-then-else branches mean within a couple of months, never mind other developers who decide to use it in their projects. The first time someone needs to change it, they’ll be better off throwing it out and writing something clearer.

And this is far from the most striking example. Just look at regular expressions for validating email addresses. Makes you want to step outside for some air, doesn’t it? :-)

Fifty Times Faster
5 December 2019 ·

Here’s the brief: a client’s month-end closing document takes just under an hour to post. The database isn’t especially big, but an hour is still way too long. Sure, you don’t close the month very often, and you could do it at night. Still.

I dig into the code, profile it, and see that the platform spends almost all that time in a single procedure, executing a query batch. I look at the first query and think: classic, accessing data through a dot on a composite type. The DBMS must be attaching a wagonload of joins to huge document tables, and the optimizer can’t come up with a decent plan in time.

I test the theory. But SalesDocument includes only eight document types. That should be manageable: the usual rule of thumb is that the optimizer can find a decent plan with up to eight joins.

I check the document tables: they aren’t particularly big. I run the query separately from the batch. It isn’t instantaneous, reading around 350,000 records and selecting about 200,000, but it certainly doesn’t take an hour.

All right, the batch’s first query is heavy, but it’s not the problem. I look at the second and realize that we’ve just read the entire Inventory register and selected most of its records, and now we’re reading it again and joining both result sets on a pile of conditions. The register’s record table has no suitable index: only the standard recorder index, which naturally doesn’t help.

I check: this is exactly where the platform spends most of its time waiting for the DBMS.

I couldn’t find a way around reading the whole register table twice. Every alternative I tried meant changing how the data was stored, and that wasn’t an option. So I went with a compromise: in the second query, I replaced the join to the actual register record table with a join to a temporary table created in advance and indexed on the join fields.

This was a case where 1C’s general recommendation worked perfectly: posting time fell from 50 minutes to three, and after further code optimization, to one minute. Fifty times faster than where I started.

A minute for month-end closing is usually fine, so I called it a day.

What Is the Performance Management Center For?
24 November 2019 ·

You use the Performance Management Center to:

  1. Find a system bottleneck, such as slow code or a heavy query;
  2. Investigate specific locks or deadlocks.

For the first one, turn on query analysis and, say, server call analysis. The results show which parts of the system load the application server and which load the DBMS server. This is often done without a specific problem, simply to remove bottlenecks and give the system more headroom for the future.

For the second, turn on lock or deadlock analysis when you know they occur and want a report: who blocked whom, when, on which line of code, and so forth.

In both cases, monitoring runs only during peak load, for ten to fifteen minutes. That keeps the pile of raw data manageable. PMC has to chew through it before it can show you anything, and the more you collect, the longer that takes. You also avoid picking up unrelated stuff, like load from overnight maintenance jobs.

It also keeps the collection itself from slowing things down too much. PMC can collect a monster of a technological log, and your hardware will feel it. Thirty percent slower? Hold my beer. Be careful with that.

PMC’s analytical indicators are sufficient for all of the above: query analysis, lock waits, and 1C and MS SQL deadlock analysis. Operational indicators, such as the number of queries running and their total execution time, are less popular. They usually aren’t worth the time it takes to set them up, and PMC was never really designed to collect them continuously.

What Is Bablox?
20 October 2019 ·

I watched Evgeny Filippov’s webinar about Bablox. Basically, it’s another way to measure performance. Like Apdex, it relies on timing operations, but uses a different calculation.

To calculate Bablox, multiply an operation’s duration by the salary rate of the user performing it. The salary can be:

  • An average value, if you want a rough performance comparison of the same application across several companies.
  • The user’s actual salary, if you need to convince management to spend some money on making things faster.

You end up with a figure for how much money the business has lost to a slow application. That’s the big selling point: it’s a number the average CFO can get their head around. Explaining what an Apdex of 0.5 means takes some effort; explaining a loss of 300,000 rubles doesn’t.

It also takes the guesswork out of questions that come up in every implementation. Take deciding which operations matter most: which matters more, selling goods faster or receiving them into the warehouse? Once you know how much money the company loses on each operation, the answer is much easier.

Of course, it’s not a perfect model. Suppose the application is slow for warehouse workers but runs fine for accountants. Warehouse workers earn less, so their Bablox will be low. But accountants depend on what the warehouse workers enter. Until that’s done, they have nothing to work with. The company is losing money because the application is slow for warehouse workers, but Bablox won’t show it.

I doubt Bablox will knock Apdex off its perch in the IT world, but it’s an interesting idea, and it could make talking to clients a whole lot easier.

A Large 1C Implementation
15 October 2019 ·

What counts as a large 1C implementation? In Russia, the platform is used almost everywhere, even in companies that use a lot of competing software, like SAP. Of course, some implementations are small, with 1C handling purely practical tasks like generating reports. But the Corporate Technology Support Center’s work includes truly enormous projects, such as optimizing the Delovye Linii system for five thousand concurrent users.

So in Russia these days, hundreds of people working in the same infobase at once is a medium-sized implementation. A thousand or more is a large one.

The size of the database doesn’t tell you much on its own: many configurations don’t involve large numbers of concurrent users. A classic example is 1C:Document Management; a less classic one is Avibus’s Bus Terminal Management. Bus Terminal Management can collect huge amounts of data in its central database from remote nodes in its distributed network of bus terminals and stations, without having many users working simultaneously.

A Turnover Register without Turnovers
15 October 2019 ·

If you disable “Use in totals” for every dimension of a turnover register, its turnovers will no longer be calculated. In fact, the turnover table disappears from the database altogether. Try to query it in 1C, and you’ll get an error.

That can come in handy when all we do is collect data, then filter it by recorder or other fields. We only need the register’s record table. There’s no point spending server resources calculating and storing a turnover table.

An information register naturally comes to mind for this task. But its efficiency depends on how many dimensions you plan to create: every index on an information register includes all its dimensions, plus the period for periodic registers. The platform creates a base dimension index, an index for each dimension marked “Master,” and an index for each dimension, resource, or attribute you choose to index separately. And we haven’t even reached the slice tables, which use the same approach!

So if your information register isn’t thought through all that well and has quite a few dimensions, say more than two or three, keeping all those indexes up to date can get expensive. A “flat” turnover register without turnovers starts to look pretty good.

My well-read friends sometimes ask what my favorite book is. And, damn it, I always feel a bit embarrassed answering, because out of all the books in the world, it’s Andy Weir’s The Martian.
